BBC World News Digest: Israel carries out attack against a Hamas leader in Gaza
Global News Podcast.
Israel announced it has killed a Hamas architect behind the October 7th attacks. The emergency services in Gaza City say Israeli strikes killed at least seven people. A Palestinian Civil Defense spokesperson stated the attack killed civilians. Witnesses reported a building inhabited by citizens was targeted by three missiles, and a fleeing car was hit nearby. Izzedine ul Haddad, described as the last living mastermind of the October 7th attacks, was a prominent Hamas leader. Israel accuses him of responsibility for murder, kidnap, and injury of Israeli citizens and troops. The attacks tonight are believed to have impacted Hamas's leadership and ability to strategize.
Israel and Lebanon have agreed to extend their ceasefire. However, cross-border strikes between Israel and the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah are continuing. This ceasefire has been in place for about a month and is now extended for another 45 days. Despite this, violence continues with widespread Israeli attacks and casualties on both sides.
After a two-day summit with China's President Xi, President Trump is back in Washington. Trump described the summit as fantastic, saying great deals and relationships were made. China's Foreign Ministry stated trade would be expanded under reciprocal tariff reductions. One confirmed outcome is Boeing's agreement to sell 200 aircraft to China. Iran was also on the agenda, but President Trump did not ask for a favor regarding the Strait of Hormuz, suggesting China's own interests could lead to its reopening. No breakthrough on this issue was reported.
Politicians in Australia's Northern Territory have announced a review into the child protection system after the death of a five-year-old Aboriginal girl in Alice Springs. Kumanjayi little baby, as she's known for cultural reasons, went missing last month, and a 47-year-old man has been charged with her murder. Her death caused national outrage and grief, highlighting deep disparities in Australia. Historically, Australian governments' policies have failed Aboriginal people, including the forced removal of thousands of children to assimilate them, known as the Stolen Generations. In 2007, a Northern Territory intervention was aimed at combating alleged child sexual abuse in Aboriginal communities. Liberal Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price highlighted the silence around what is happening in remote communities, a silence driven by fear of being labeled racist, which she said is killing babies. Leaders emphasize that Aboriginal people should not be blamed for these failings and must be consulted to find a way forward, not just in child protection, but also in housing, justice, and the prison system.
In Bolivia, since May, people have been protesting against the austerity policies of the center-right President Rodrigo Paz. Protests turned violent with explosions and tear gas as miners called for him to resign. The Bolivian government has now reached a deal with protesting miners after nearly 12 hours of negotiations. Most of the miners' demands were addressed, including access to further equipment and explosives. However, the government is still grappling with protests from other workers, such as teachers and transportation workers, demanding wage increases and better working conditions. The political turmoil continues, fueled by the economy and a severe funding and foreign exchange crisis the country faced when President Paz took power in November. His austerity and privatization measures, including scrapping fuel subsidies, have increased costs and sparked discontent, especially among indigenous communities worried about big businesses taking over their land.
The World Health Organization is calling for countries to do more to restrict the sale of nicotine pouches to young people. The WHO warns that deceptive marketing tactics are driving a rapid rise in their consumption among young people worldwide, creating the risk of a new generation of nicotine addicts. Manufacturers are accused of using bright packaging and sweet flavors, like bubblegum and gummy bears, and promoting the pouches through social media influencers to offset falling smoking rates. Currently, only 16 countries ban them outright, and 32 regulate them in some way.
The celebrated French art museum, the Musée d'Orsay in Paris, is holding an unusual exhibition: it features impressionist masterpieces by Renoir and Degas, as well as a sculpture by Rodin, that it desperately wants to give away. All of the works were stolen by the Nazis during the occupation of France in the Second World War. They were subsequently recovered from Germany or Austria, but none of their former owners have claimed them back. David Zivi, a French Culture Ministry official, explained that identifying original owners is complex due to a lack of complete data and the passage of over 80 years. Many works were stolen from Jewish families, some were seized or sold under duress during the war, or even sold by owners needing funds to escape. While an Allied army team, the Monument Men, recovered items, and French Fine Arts officers also documented looted works, it remains challenging to trace ownership. The museum hopes that surviving archival pieces or photographs might help descendants recognize the artworks. Success would mean these artworks find their rightful homes.
The hunt for the next James Bond has officially kicked off. Amazon MGM Studios, which now controls the Bond franchise, is reportedly looking for a younger actor with a "Goldilocks amount of fame." Daniel Craig was the most commercially successful and critically successful James Bond. Speculation includes British actors such as Harris Dickinson and Lewis Partridge. The role is significant as Bond is seen as a global cultural hero, representing what people expect from a British hero.

Bloomberg The Big Take: The Biggest Takeaways from the Trump-Xi Summit
Welcome to The Big Take from Bloomberg News. Today on the show, Big Take Asia host Juan Ha takes listeners inside the Trump-Xi summit. What the visit did and didn't accomplish. And what to watch for as Trump and Xi navigate Iran and China's ambitions in Taiwan.
Jeff Mason and John Liu, welcome. This summit marks the first visit by a sitting US President to China in nearly a decade. A lot has changed in the US-China relationship since Trump's 2017 visit, including COVID, spy balloons, and trade wars. While COVID initially soured President Trump on China, he now seems more focused on business deals and gaining support from President Xi regarding the Iran war.
Both presidents were eager to "make nice" due to their respective domestic pressures. Trump faces the war in the Middle East with Iran, while Xi's economy is struggling with deflation and export dependency. Trump’s top priority is resolving the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Though downplaying it, this issue is critical to him, impacting the global economy and US midterm elections through gasoline prices. The White House reported that President Xi agreed Iran should not have a nuclear weapon and the Strait of Hormuz should not be under Iran’s control, marking a win for the US.
China, the largest buyer of Iranian oil, has officially opposed the war but remained on the sidelines. Its main concern is the secondary economic impact of the war, as higher oil prices would reduce global demand for Chinese goods. China is reluctant to mediate, fearing blame if a resolution fails.
Taiwan, claimed by China, remains a significant balancing act. Beijing’s statement after the talks emphasized Taiwan as the most important issue in China-US relations, warning of clashes if not handled properly. While Xi consistently raises Taiwan, this summit uniquely featured a clear linkage to potential conflict, signaling a "higher volume" to his message. Despite concerns that Trump might make major concessions on Taiwan for business or Iran support, this did not appear to happen. Each side focused on its own agenda; China on Taiwan, the US on Iran, often talking past each other.
At the previous leaders' meeting, tariffs were central. This time, the US Supreme Court ruling against Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs constrained his leverage. Despite this, Trump still intends to use tariffs, promising alternative legal avenues. The summit appears to be a reset after a tense year. It's also the first of four potential meetings between Trump and Xi this year, including Xi’s US visits in September and December for the G20, and a Trump visit to China in November for APEC. This sets up a year of intense discussion and diplomacy.
Xi opened the meeting by citing the "Thucydides Trap"—the inevitable conflict when a rising power challenges an established one. He emphasized that despite fundamental differences in political systems, economics, and social norms, leaders have a "choice" over "fate." He urged proactive management of the relationship to prevent it from falling into conflict.
This is The Big Take from Bloomberg News.

item.title: Wall Street Journal The Journal: Musk vs. Altman
item.itunes:title: Wall Street Journal The Journal: Musk vs. Altman
item.description:
Wall Street Journal The Journal: Musk vs. Altman
The US Courthouse in Oakland, California, was the venue for a high-stakes trial over OpenAI, with a crowd of people gathered outside daily. The two people on opposite sides of the trial are Elon Musk and Sam Altman, two of the co-founders of OpenAI. The lawsuit itself is called Musk versus Altman. Elon Musk is suing OpenAI for basically manipulating him into giving tens of millions of dollars to OpenAI. Musk's initial funding helped get OpenAI off the ground. Essentially, he says OpenAI and Sam Altman as its leader misused those donations because the company abandoned its original mission of building AI for the good of humanity. As the trial has unfolded over the past three weeks, a who's who of Silicon Valley have filed into the courthouse, headed for the witness stand. As soon as they come into the security, all these photographers and videographers just start clamoring up against the windows. As the day goes on, protestors start showing up outside the courthouse. Closing arguments for the trial happened yesterday, and a verdict could come as soon as next week. Some of the things Musk wants are for Sam Altman to be removed as OpenAI CEO, and for the company to transfer around 180 billion dollars to its charitable arm. If even one of these is granted, that could really upend OpenAI as it is today. For OpenAI, the stakes are very high. Today is Friday, May 15th. Coming up on the show is the blockbuster AI trial of the century.
The roots of this lawsuit go back to OpenAI's origins. The company was founded in 2015, and its goal was to build technology for the good of humanity. OpenAI was started as a non-profit so that no one entity, no one person, no one company would control very powerful technology. Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and the other founders wanted to create AI that was safe, so that it didn't destroy all humankind. They also wanted to be driven by their ideas, not by shareholders and profit. To help get the project off the ground, they got donations from several tech players, including 38 million dollars from Elon Musk. It wasn't enough, because it turns out that building AI is really, really expensive. Companies need billions for the computing power to train models and make them better. OpenAI's leaders came to feel that as a non-profit, the company simply wouldn't be able to raise enough to fund their ambitions. So they restructured into a for-profit. That let them start bringing in investments, though the company still has a non-profit parent. With the for-profit conversion, you now got a CEO who's got shareholders to answer to. The incentives have completely shifted, is what some people would argue. Since then, OpenAI has grown exponentially. It's formed a partnership with Microsoft, and the company's latest valuation puts it at over 800 billion dollars.
Meanwhile, Musk's relationship with the company had started to deteriorate. Musk left OpenAI's board in 2018 and later founded his own AI company, XAI. He's also become publicly critical of both OpenAI and Altman. Musk gave an analogy, stating that it would be like if you funded an organization to save the Amazon rainforest and instead they became a lumber company and chopped down the forest and sold it for money. Musk took his disagreement with OpenAI one step further when in 2024, he filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, Altman, and the company's president, Greg Brockman. Elon Musk is suing OpenAI and the company's CEO, Sam Altman, alleging they have breached the company's founding agreement by putting profits ahead of its original promise, which was to do good for the public. It took a while for the suit to get to trial, but it finally started a few weeks ago at the end of April.
The judge for this trial is Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. She has presided in a lot of really important cases that have had a lot of ramifications for Silicon Valley, and she has a reputation for being a real no-nonsense judge. She lived up to that reputation almost right away. On the day of opening arguments, she reprimanded Musk for posting about the trial on social media and called him up to the podium. She had the richest man in the world step up to the courtroom and basically look up at her. She basically said, 'Your posting on X is causing me trouble. Maybe you've never done this before, but let's see if you can actually stop posting on X for once in your life.' Musk had to say, 'Yes, I'll stop posting.'
Let's get into the two sides of this trial, starting with Musk's side. Musk's lawyers are essentially saying that Sam and Greg were not truthful about their intentions when they created OpenAI. And that as Elon was giving tens of millions of dollars to OpenAI, Sam and Greg's intentions were to turn into a for-profit and make a lot of money from it. One of the most striking pieces of evidence that Musk's team presented was the personal journal of OpenAI's president, Greg Brockman. With Greg, Musk's lawyers have pointed to some private journal entries that he had written during that time when they were negotiating the for-profit conversion, to basically show the jurors, 'Look, Greg has always just been in this for the money. He didn't care about the mission.' Excerpts from Brockman's journal, which were written in a kind of shorthand, were displayed on large video screens, big enough for the whole courtroom to see. While OpenAI lawyers referred to Brockman's journal, Musk's lawyers repeatedly called it a diary. In one journal entry, he wrote, 'Financially, what will take me to 1 billion?' This implies he already had an interest in making money at the time. Musk's lawyers really made the most out of these diary entries for their argument. Steven Molo, litigator for Musk, brought up that particular passage, 'Financially, what will take me to 1 billion?' And then he asked Brockman when he was on the witness stand, 'What you really wanted was to be a billionaire, right?' Greg afterward said, 'Solving for the mission has always been my primary motivation and it remains so today.' Musk's team pointed to another entry from Brockman's journal where he wrote about turning OpenAI into a for-profit and what it would mean for Musk. It reads, 'It'd be wrong to steal the nonprofit from him,' and also, 'That'd be pretty morally bankrupt, and he's not really an idiot.' Musk's lawyers were trying to say that Greg has always just been in this for the money; he didn't care about the mission. This is very unusual as a piece of evidence in a trial like this. The way that Greg has described it is that this was never meant for public consumption. And he has described it as his stream of consciousness, that there are things that he wrote that maybe he didn't really mean. It was just a passing thought. But now it's been put up for evidence.
When one OpenAI board member was on the stand, the judge asked about what's more important: the fiduciary duty to the for-profit or the mission of the non-profit. The board member said the mission always takes precedence. Over the course of the trial, a number of other big Silicon Valley names testified, like Satya Nadella, the CEO of Microsoft, Ilya Sutskever, another co-founder of OpenAI, and Shivon Zilis, a former OpenAI board member and Musk's current romantic partner. And there was Elon Musk himself, who was on the stand for three days. At one point he said, 'I was a fool who provided them free funding to create a startup.' Then, as the trial moved into its third week, all eyes turned to one of the final witnesses, Sam Altman.
On the other side, OpenAI's lawyers are arguing that Elon is for the for-profit conversion. Not only was Elon for the for-profit conversion, he actually wanted majority control of it. And that when the OpenAI co-founders said no to that request, Elon cut off funding, went on to start his own AI company, and that this lawsuit is the latest variant of Elon's efforts to basically slow OpenAI down for his own AI company, painting him as a vindictive person. They pointed to a number of emails and text messages that pointed to Musk's approval of the for-profit conversion. Musk's defense against that was that, 'Yes, I was for a for-profit conversion at one point because I understood that they needed more financing. I just don't agree with how they went about it.' OpenAI's lawyer said that no promises were made to Musk that OpenAI would remain a non-profit organization. He said, 'The only person who claims to have heard these promises is Mr. Musk himself.' On Tuesday morning, OpenAI's lawyers called their star witness, Sam Altman. He walked into the courtroom wearing a sharp suit and lavender tie. Altman kept a pretty calm demeanor throughout the entire time of the trial. Sam was actually in the courtroom for most of the days during this trial, but Tuesday was his first day actually on the witness stand. Part of the Musk team's courtroom strategy was to prove that Altman was untrustworthy, that he had lied to the company's board a number of times, and that he prioritized profit over the company's original mission. If they can prove to the jurors that this is an untrustworthy person, then they can make the case that Sam had ill intent all along. While a lot of these accusations of Sam lying didn't necessarily pertain to the for-profit conversion, it still paints this picture of Sam being a liar. Altman's lawyers wanted him to show that wasn't true and to make that case directly to the jurors. When he testified, he talked about his upbringing, how he got into the tech industry, and how he helped start OpenAI. At some point during his testimony, the infamous blip came up, which was the unexpected firing of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, the short period of time when Sam was ousted as CEO and then he came back. The board says it pushed Altman out after a review found he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board. OpenAI posted on X that Sam Altman would now officially return as CEO. That was an important moment in Sam's testimony because it was his time to tell the jurors his perspective of the events that happened. As we all know now, the board then felt the need to push Sam out because they said that he hadn't been honest with them about a number of things. Sam said there was clearly a misunderstanding, and there was clearly a breach of trust, and he apologized for that. Then Musk's lawyer, Steven Molo, took his turn questioning Altman. The cross-examination had a very fiery start. The first question that Musk's litigator asked him was, 'Are you completely trustworthy?' And Sam said, 'I believe so.' And Molo said, 'But you don't know whether you're completely trustworthy.' So that was really how the cross-examination started. It set the tone. Shortly after that, Molo brought up specific testimonies that actually came up during the trial. Sam would say, 'Oh, I didn't watch that deposition. I didn't listen to that testimony.' And at a certain point, Molo said, 'Are you even paying attention in this trial? Like, do you even care about this trial?' And Sam had a very long pause, and then he said, 'Of course I care, but I'm also running a very important company.' Sam's legal team very much called this cross-examination a character assassination. That's how they described it in a press conference after Sam's testimony.
The trial wrapped up yesterday with closing arguments. OpenAI's lawyers said Musk was aware of the plan to convert the company from a non-profit to a for-profit and only soured on the idea once it became clear he couldn't fully control it. Musk's lawyer ended his arguments by reiterating that Sam Altman was a liar and that OpenAI's leadership had been deceptive. The jury is set to begin deliberations on Monday. If they decide against OpenAI, then the judge will decide what happens next, whether to give Musk any of the remedies he asked for in the original suit. Elon has asked to remove Sam as CEO and Greg as President. So it could mean OpenAI potentially losing two of its prime leaders. Another remedy that Elon is asking is for 180 billion dollars to be paid out from OpenAI's for-profit entity into its non-profit parent. There's also the potential that OpenAI would have to change its company structure. That could mean big trouble for OpenAI, which is planning to go public later this year. Being able to finance the type of data infrastructure is very, very expensive. And 180 billion dollars, it would be a huge loss for OpenAI. Any billion in loss is a huge loss for companies like these. The company's trying to go public this year, so this kind of a financial loss would seriously slow the company down. What if OpenAI wins? If OpenAI wins, then all goes according to plan. There are a lot of people who are anticipating the company's IPO. So that timeline will be cemented, and Sam will live another day as CEO of OpenAI. In other words, if the verdict goes to OpenAI, things mostly stay the same for the company. But there's now a question of whether there will be real reputational damage, and if it will stick.
What does this mean for the AI sector beyond just OpenAI and Musk? It raises some serious questions around governance. It's been really interesting to watch these very powerful people in AI, to see how they actually do deals and the consequences of their deal-making. And it brings into question who we actually want to lead these AI companies. Because neither side has painted the other leader of the next frontier of technology in a very positive light. So it brings up a lot of questions about all these people who are leading the most powerful tech companies in the world. How do we hold them accountable? Do we get a say in who leads these companies? Is this trial potentially the only way for nine very ordinary Americans who are serving as jurors to potentially have a say in who leads the most powerful AI company in the world?
News Corp, the owner of The Wall Street Journal, has a content licensing partnership with OpenAI. That's all for today, Friday, May 15th. Additional reporting in this episode by Ben Cohen, Kich Hegi, and Becky Peterson. The Journal is a co-production of Spotify and The Wall Street Journal. The show's made by Laura Ben-Shoff, Catherine Breuer, Evelyn Fajardo Alvarez, Tia Gothgari, Max Green, Sophie Cotner, Mac Kwang, Colin MacNalty, Laura Morris, Enrique Perez De La Rosa, Sara Platt, Alan Rodriguez Espinosa, Heather Rogers, Pierce Singi, Jiva Kavarma, Catherine Waylen, Tatiana Zamis, and me, Jessica Mendoza. Our engineers are Griffin Tanner, Nathan Singh, and Peter Leonard. Our theme music is by So Whiley. Additional music this week from Catherine Anderson, Peter Leonard, Emma Munger, Nathan Singh, Griffin Tanner, and Blue Dot Sessions. Fact checking this week by Mary Mathes. Thanks for listening. See you on Monday.

Today on the AI Daily Brief.
The significance of Codex coming to ChatGPT Mobile. The difference between consumer and work AI. And what to expect from Google's IO event next week.
Before that in the headlines.
Cerebras experienced a massive first day of trading, with its stock doubling and reaching a $66 billion market cap. The AI IPO market is heating up, with SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI all preparing listings amid intense demand. Figma's stock recovered from a 50% drop, crediting AI features for a 46% revenue growth. Nvidia is quietly surging, up 20% in seven days, nearing a $6 trillion valuation.
OpenAI is reportedly considering suing Apple over their ChatGPT integration, as Apple integrates Claude and Gemini internally instead. Anthropic is securing $30 billion at a $900 billion valuation, significantly ahead of OpenAI's previous valuation. Microsoft is canceling Claude code licenses to shift developers to GitHub Copilot, aiming to cut costs and boost in-house tools. Claude's Mythos showcased strong cybersecurity, exploiting macOS and patching numerous Mozilla bugs, with updated versions performing significantly better in benchmarks.
OpenAI released Codex on the ChatGPT mobile app, allowing full agentic work within the app and signaling a shift towards persistent AI operators. A growing divergence highlights consumer AI's often-unwanted features versus work AI's insatiable demand for models and tokens. Google's upcoming IO event is poised to reveal its strategy for managing both consumer and work AI, a dual focus it has historically maintained.
Google is set to introduce Gemini Spark, an always-on personal AI agent leveraging user data across its services. Gemini Spark faces both excitement for its personalized capabilities and skepticism, echoing Google's past AI assistant promises. The actual utility of personal AI agents is debated, with concerns over "context bleed" from excessive personal data affecting their efficacy.
Google is rumored to launch Gemini 3.2 Flash, a powerful and cost-effective work AI model potentially matching GPT-5.5 at 15-20x lower cost and sub-200ms latency. Clarity on Google's core AI harness for its ecosystem remains a critical unknown, unlike OpenAI and Anthropic's established platforms. Google's IO announcements might confuse markets expecting bleeding-edge models but could offer significant value to builders through consolidated, cost-effective tools.

BBC World News Digest: Trump hails 'fantastic' new trade deals with China
The China-US summit concluded with no major deals. Separately, American media reports the US is preparing to indict former Cuban President Raul Castro.
A large prisoner swap occurred between Ukraine and Russia, brokered by the US and UAE, even as both sides intensify aerial attacks.
In the Democratic Republic of Congo, health officials confirmed an Ebola outbreak in the east, with 65 deaths reported.
The Superpower Summit between the US and China wrapped up with few concrete details. President Trump claimed China would buy 200 Boeing jets, a claim not confirmed by Beijing.
On his return, Trump revealed President Xi pressed him to halt arm sales to Taiwan. Trump maintained a non-committal stance on defending Taiwan if attacked, saying only he knows his true position.
Trump confirmed additional trade deals, including China's commitment to purchase up to 950 Boeing aircraft and billions in US agricultural goods.
Adding to diplomatic intrigue, President Putin is set to visit China next week, a pre-planned trip now layered with post-summit significance.
The optics of Xi embracing Putin after Trump's departure were highlighted. Xi reportedly offered Trump a rare tour of Zhongnanhai, a privilege previously extended only to Putin.
Trump also publicly commented on Xi's physical appearance, noting he was "tall." This received no public reaction on tightly controlled Chinese social media.
US media indicates the United States is moving to indict former Cuban President Raul Castro for the 1996 downing of a humanitarian plane. This coincides with CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Havana for high-level meetings.
Correspondent Will Grant explained Castro, still influential, faces charges over the 1996 incident. The simultaneous CIA visit underscores heightened US focus on Cuba amidst a worsening economic crisis, exacerbated by a five-month US oil blockade.
Trump has even suggested a "friendly takeover" of Cuba, a comment drawing parallels to recent US actions in Venezuela.
In Ukraine, a significant prisoner exchange, brokered by the US and UAE, saw 205 soldiers released from both sides, including Mariupol defenders. This swap came amidst renewed, large-scale aerial attacks by Russia on Ukrainian cities.
The Ebola outbreak in DRC's Ituri province has led to 65 reported deaths. The region's ongoing conflict and martial law status are complicating efforts to contain the virus and identify its specific strain for treatment.
A BBC investigation uncovered AI-generated social media videos promoting anti-immigration sentiments in the UK. These sophisticated, convincing videos, produced by accounts in countries like Sri Lanka and Vietnam, exploit political outrage to advance ideological and commercial agendas.
On a positive AI note, singer-songwriter Samuel Smith, facing Parkinson's, utilized AI to transform his sung lyrics into musical arrangements. He advocates for AI as an empowering tool for creativity and rehabilitation, urging transparent discussions on its ethical use and ownership.

New York Times Hard Fork: A.I. Safety Is So Back + Mythos Mayhem with Nikesh Arora + Hot Mess Express
Welcome to an intellectually charged briefing from Hard Fork, where the landscape of AI governance, cybersecurity, and global power dynamics is undergoing a seismic, and often contradictory, transformation. This episode peels back the layers of a bewildering policy pivot, revealing the "dirty secrets" of our digital infrastructure and the human toll of an accelerating technological frontier.
The central narrative is the Trump administration's remarkable volte-face on AI safety. Just a few years ago, concerns about AI were dismissed as "domer fearmongering," a "ridiculous" agenda driven by "hyped-up fears" to enact "regulatory capture." Yet, as one guest pointedly noted, the "Trump administration's view of AI just did not survive contact with reality." This shift is underscored by a new executive order—still in flux—aimed at creating an AI working group and a formal government review process for new models. This marks a stark departure from the administration's previous stance, which, by cancelling President Biden's similar executive order, had been perceived as "anti-innovation" and a push to "win the AI race" by letting "the labs do whatever they want." Now, the "shoe is on the other foot," and suddenly, they're "quite scared about what's happening."
This policy reversal has a proximate cause: Anthropic's Claude Mythos model. Released in a preview to a select group of federal agencies and companies, Mythos is "very good, apparently, at finding novel vulnerabilities in code that can be used to create exploits." This capability has exposed a "vast amount of harm" lurking in existing software. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora vividly describes it as initiating a "great cleansing" of the "vulnerability debt" that humans have been accumulating for "a very long time." Companies like Mozilla are now reporting "hundreds of bugs" discovered in mere weeks, a rate "five to seven times" higher than typical. The implication is profound: if a cybersecurity firm can find these vulnerabilities, so can malicious actors. This revelation has pushed the administration to confront the reality that "these models are very powerful, and we don't want our adversaries to get access to them."
The geopolitical stakes are equally high. The US-China tech rivalry takes center stage, with reports of China actively seeking access to Mythos-level capabilities. This creates an "inherently contradictory" situation where the US might both sell chips that enable China to develop its own advanced AI while simultaneously trying to block access to existing powerful models. This "AI brinksmanship" extends globally, with countries like Germany demanding access to state-of-the-art models for their own national security. The question of "who should have access to which models when" is now a global dilemma, marking a new era of "unbalanced fight" where defenders must be right 100% of the time, while attackers only need to succeed once.
Beyond policy, the cyber threat landscape is accelerating at an alarming rate. Google recently identified an attacker using a "zero-day exploit" developed with AI – a "grim milestone." Even the seemingly benign act of managing an online learning platform has been disrupted by cyberattacks forcing negotiations with hackers. This escalation impacts everyone, especially "non-tech businesses" like hospitals, which rely heavily on technology but may lack the resources and expertise of tech giants.
Amidst this tumult, the human element emerges. Tech employees are caught between the excitement of powerful new tools and the anxiety of intensified workloads. The polarization around AI safety has created a toxic environment where sincere concerns were once dismissed as "hysterical liberals" seeking "heavy-handed regulation." Now, with the undeniable evidence of AI's power, there's a desperate scramble to catch up. The irony is palpable, with the very people who once derided "AI safety" now leading the charge. This extends to personal cybersecurity, where the sophistication of phishing attacks, potentially AI-assisted, threatens to make even savvy users vulnerable, necessitating a re-evaluation of basic digital hygiene. As one guest humorously but pointedly observed about email security: "You're telling me it's hard for the email provider to figure out that this is not an X email address? I mean, these are the same guys that are building AI, right?"
The question remains: who wins in this race between AI's potential and its perils? For now, the answer is "entirely confused and incoherent." But one thing is clear: the "Overton window has shifted" with remarkable speed, forcing a reckoning with AI's power that the world can no longer ignore.
(Audio briefing concludes)

The Economist The Intelligence: Top dog-whistler: Tommy Robinson and Britain’s far right
Hello and welcome to The Intelligence from The Economist.
First up today, we explore the continuing influence of Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, widely known as the far-right activist Tommy Robinson. This Saturday, he is set to host what he calls the "biggest patriotic gathering" in London. Robinson maintains a significant online presence with 1.9 million followers on X and has garnered support from influential figures in America, including Donald Trump's former strategist Steve Bannon and Elon Musk, who once paid his legal fees. He presents a "distorted vision of Britain," often warning of radical Islam and framing immigration as an invasion, though critics view his rhetoric as bigoted. His image as a free-speech martyr resonates particularly with the American right and disillusioned Britons who mistrust mainstream government and media. However, despite his popularity, his influence has not translated into electoral success, as seen in his failed bid for European Parliament in 2019. The upcoming rally is expected to feature international figures, even as the British government has controversially banned some speakers. Robinson's strategy involves sanitizing a message that many find deeply worrying, effectively reframing complex issues like immigration into simplified narratives of invasion.
Next, we turn to a significant development in the elevator industry. Two major players, Finland's Kone and Germany's TK Elevator – formerly Thyssenkrupp's lift division – have announced a multi-billion dollar merger. This new combined entity is set to be valued at nearly 30 billion euros, immediately elevating it to the number one position globally, surpassing long-standing market leader Otis, with an estimated 28% market share. The primary driver behind this consolidation is the pursuit of economies of scale, particularly in the lucrative areas of servicing and modernizing existing lifts, especially in China. Modern cityscapes are fundamentally reliant on elevators, making them an indispensable form of transport. However, competitors like Otis and Schindler have expressed strong concerns about the increased market concentration, with one executive calling the merger a "blood bath" and urging antitrust authorities worldwide to scrutinize the deal.
Finally, we pay tribute to Rahul Rai, India's most celebrated photojournalist, who has passed away at the age of 83. Rai was renowned for his extraordinary ability to perceive and capture moments that others overlooked, consistently seeking "revelatory moments" – a single, powerful image to encapsulate an entire subject. His journey into photography began as an adult civil engineer, inspired by a published photo of a donkey foal. Rai is particularly famous for two impactful photo essays that documented immense human suffering. The first covered the Bangladesh Independence War in 1971, where he captured the plight of refugees. The second, and perhaps most iconic, chronicled the devastating Bhopal disaster of 1984. Faced with the overwhelming scale, Rai eventually captured the haunting image of a recently buried child's face, with the father's hand brushing away earth – a photograph that became the defining symbol of the Bhopal catastrophe. Throughout his career, Varanasi, the holy city on the Ganges, was his favorite place to photograph. He believed that while others sought spiritual fulfillment through rituals, he found his own "Dharma" by walking among the people with his camera.
That's all for this episode of The Intelligence.

New York Times The Daily: Lessons From the Hantavirus Outbreak
We open on the claustrophobic reality of quarantine, through the eyes of a listener on a quarantined cruise ship, isolated in an Omaha unit. The daily temperature checks and the ever-present mask are stark reminders of a global anxiety that now fixates on a specific outbreak aboard another vessel. This isn't just any virus; it's Hantavirus, a name that, for many, evokes a primordial fear, and for good reason: it’s a "little understood disease" with a "highly fatal" outcome once contracted.
The narrative unravels the tragic events on a polar expedition cruise. It began with a Dutch couple, likely infected by a specific long-tailed pygmy rat in Argentina. The husband died swiftly, and days later, his wife, after disembarking in South Africa, succumbed as well. This was no ordinary death; it marked the emergence of the Andes species of Hantavirus, capable of human-to-human transmission—a critical detail that initially seemed to escape the public health narrative.
As more passengers fell ill, and a third, seemingly unconnected person died, the initial "think horses not zebras" complacency shattered. The virus, characterized by severe respiratory illness culminating in pneumonia and immune system overdrive, has no treatment. Its R-naught of 2.1, while modest compared to Measles or Omicron, signifies a level of transmissibility beyond initial cautious statements. Moreover, the fatality rate, hovering around 30% in both this and a prior Argentinian outbreak, underscores its lethal potential.
Yet, amid this unfolding crisis, the public health communication struck a dissonant chord. Driven by a palpable "post-Covid PTSD," officials, including the acting CDC director, urged calm, insisting on close, sustained contact for transmission. This reassurance, while perhaps well-intentioned to prevent panic, was, as one reporter observed, a "missing nuance." Research, notably from a 2018 Argentina outbreak, showed transmission could occur even "in passing," challenging the official narrative.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention itself remained conspicuously silent for days, a delay exacerbated by past political tensions that fractured its relationship with the WHO. While the CDC is now fully engaged and effectively managing the situation, this initial hesitancy and the subsequent downplaying of risks represent a profound misstep. The core lesson here isn't about the virus itself, but about the enduring failure in transparent communication. In an outbreak, "time is everything."
Those who once rightly criticized previous administrations for withholding information or making claims without evidence are now inadvertently repeating similar patterns. The public demands to be treated "like adults," expecting honesty about what is known, what isn't, and the uncertainties that persist. Without that candid dialogue, the trust essential to navigating future, potentially more devastating, outbreaks will remain dangerously eroded.

Wall Street Journal The Journal: Jerome Powell’s Last Stand at the Fed
Jerome Powell was originally slated to retire quietly, anticipating a life of golf, guitar, and time with family. His exit plan was simple: less monetary policy, more Hank Williams. Many expected his last day as Fed Chair to be tomorrow.
However, weeks before that anticipated departure, Powell made an announcement. He would step down as chair, but in a significant break from over 75 years of Fed tradition, he would not leave the Fed entirely. His term as chair would end on May 15, but he intended to continue serving as a governor.
Critics quickly denounced this move as a violation of Federal Reserve norms and a threat to Fed independence. Powell stated he had no other option, explaining that recent events left him with no choice but to stay to protect the institution, especially given the strained relationship between the Federal Reserve and the executive branch.
According to Nick Timiraos, who has covered Powell for a decade, Powell possesses an unusual talent: the ability to repeat sentences backward. Nick believes this skill highlights Powell's exceptional listening ability, which he has used to build relationships with colleagues and politicians. Powell himself once joked about wearing out the carpets of Capitol Hill through constant meetings.
The strain between Powell and then-President Donald Trump began months after Trump appointed him. In 2018, as the Fed raised interest rates to cool an overheating economy, Trump grew increasingly hostile, even discussing firing Powell after four rate increases. Federal law, however, only permits removing a Fed governor for cause.
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, the Fed, under Powell, became a first responder. It slashed rates to zero, pumped money into the financial system, and even directly lent to businesses—unprecedented actions that earned Powell widespread praise, including from Trump.
After President Biden reappointed Powell in 2021, new challenges emerged. Snarled supply chains and rising demand led to inflation, which the Fed initially miscalculated by keeping rates too low for too long. By late 2021, the Fed realized its error and began rapidly raising rates—the fastest increases in four decades—which helped bring down inflation but made borrowing more expensive.
This misread had political fallout. Republicans accused the Fed of timing rate cuts to benefit the Biden administration before the 2024 election. When Trump returned to office in 2025, he resumed his pressure on Powell, threatening to fire him. When that proved difficult, he targeted other Fed board members, attempting to remove a Biden-appointed governor using unproven allegations. The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation into Powell over building renovations.
Nick Timiraos suggests these actions aimed to pressure the Fed to lower interest rates. While a White House spokeswoman denied Trump directed the investigation, lawmakers from both parties saw it as political interference. The Justice Department eventually dropped the probe, but Nick argues it fundamentally altered Powell's retirement plans. He believes Powell's decision to stay was to act as a firewall, protecting the institution from political influence and preventing a deeper fracture.
Powell's continued presence creates an awkward situation, particularly for incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who had previously campaigned publicly against Powell's leadership. Powell's decision to stay also denies Trump a key appointment on the evenly split seven-member Fed Board of Governors.
The current Fed is increasingly divided, with recent meetings showing the most dissension since 1992. This uncertainty, coupled with new data showing inflation picking back up due to rising energy prices, means rate cuts are off the table for now. The economy is shifting again, putting the Fed in a tough spot where it may have to say no to White House demands for lower interest rates.
Looking ahead, Powell’s legacy will likely be defined by his decision to challenge a president's attempt to control monetary policy. If the Fed's independence survives, his legacy will be seen favorably.

Lehane acknowledged that AI companies will be crushed by public sentiment if they don't find a way to redistribute AI wealth, similar to how Alaska shares oil and gas revenue with citizens. He stated, "People need to feel like they're going to have a piece of this and participate in it. You can't talk beyond people or above people. Stop guessing if your AI investment is working. Check out Section at sectionai.com. That's S E C T I O N A I.com.
Welcome back to the AI Daily Brief. Today we are discussing the most recent changes to how paid Claude plans work. This has caused a ton of angry discussion among developers, but it reflects a much bigger shift. A couple of weeks ago, we published a show called "The AI Subsidy Era Ends," and this story is really that coming home to roost.
On Wednesday, Anthropic announced a big change to their pricing model. As of June 15th, paid users will be able to claim a monthly credit for what Anthropic calls programmatic usage. Basically, there are two different ways people use Claude: "human in the loop" where you interact with Claude via Claude AI or Claude Co-work apps, and "away from keyboard" usage, which includes the Claude Agent SDK, Claude-P from the CLI, or Claude GitHub Actions. Previously, Claude subscriptions covered both categories of usage, but now they are separating them. Anthropic is calling the "human in the loop" usage "interactive use" and "away from keyboard" usage "programmatic use."
Anthropic's account tried to present this change as a bonus, saying that existing interactive usage limits remain unchanged, and users are now getting a bonus credit for programmatic usage, equal to the amount they pay for their plan. Anthropic states this change clarifies things, officially allows third-party tools built on the Agent SDK to work with Claude plans, and provides a "free" credit.
However, for many developers, this is not a bonus. The core issue is token subsidies. For a very long time, power users have been able to use dramatically more tokens than the equivalent value of API credits in their plans. For example, some Claude Max subscribers were effectively using thousands of dollars worth of tokens for a 200 dollar a month plan. The fact that a subsidy existed was very clear. The problem is that many people have built their third-party projects around an assumption of that subsidy persisting. With this announcement, Anthropic is saying that the subsidy is persisting for people using Claude Code through their official harness, but it is not persisting if you are trying to use your Claude subscription for third-party experiences. Those experiences are now going to be billed straight on API rates.
A big chunk of the developer community absolutely crashed out at this. AI YouTuber and T3 Code builder Theo expressed feeling personally burned, having put so much work into wrapping the SDK for T3 Code, only for their users to have their rate limits cut by 40X. He warned against trusting Anthropic's statements. Robin Evers, an AI coach for founders, stated Anthropic "literally effing disgusts" him, accusing them of intentionally misleading copy and rules, and saying he was happy to cancel his subscription. Mario Zechner suggested Anthropic doesn't care about dev sentiment anymore, having reached corporate decision-makers' hearts and minds, focusing instead on "obligatory enterprise Claude Code."
Many believe these actions indicate that Anthropic is abandoning the people who got them to where they are, focusing on enterprise clients instead. This reflects a strategy of "getting the nerds to get the normies, then dropping the nerds," which is as old as computers. The affected businesses are often alternative harnesses for using Claude Code, which, developers argue, are valuable to the overall ecosystem by giving people different entry points and should be supported. Theo further criticized Anthropic for spending more time trying to lock out better apps and harnesses than fixing Claude Code itself.
Another major issue was the feeling of being gaslit and talked down to. Austin Allred, founder of Gauntlet, called out Anthropic for saying the new changes are "dramatically more expensive, but you get a few free credits towards the new expense to soften the blow." He emphasized that users are not dumb and companies should "stop trying to dress everything up in 10 layers of PR speak and just say what it is." Peter Yang advised that companies "just have to be honest and upfront about your constraints, especially with developers," as it is very hard to earn their trust and once lost, it's very hard to earn it back.
The speaker noted that while there's a lot of critique, some observers, like developer Nick Dobos, point out that "everyone with an ounce of sense knew this was coming. Did y'all seriously expect to run your insane custom scripts on top of Claude at the massively discounted subscription rate forever?"
Possible explanations for Anthropic's move include: 1. Anthropic doesn't want third-party developers around, as evidenced by past crackdowns and their bias towards getting people to use their own harnesses. 2. Anthropic is actively seeking to own the application layer, shown by updates to Claude for Legal, Finance, and the new Claude for Small Business, suggesting a more "Apple-like" approach of controlling the end-to-end experience. 3. Anthropic is flexing its pricing power, as they are becoming increasingly dominant in enterprise usage, with recent data showing them overtaking Open AI in business usage for the first time.
However, the speaker believes the core issue here is not acrimony towards third-party developers or competing harnesses, but simply "the end of the AI subsidy era." We have moved from a paradigm of caring about seats to caring about tokens. With the shift from assisted AI to agentic AI, the business model cannot be based on seats anymore, as agents can consume the equivalent usage of dozens or hundreds of seats. The speaker states that we are crashing "headlong into the inevitable market consequence of there being massively more demand for tokens than there is supply of tokens."
Anthropic has been telegraphing these changes for months, struggling with compute and latency, and being a victim of their own success. All signs have been pointing to the end of these subsidies. For example, Claude Code's Tariq wrote in February that if you're building a business on top of the Agent SDK, you should use an API key instead.
The previous subsidies were significant. One example showed a developer using 31 dollars worth of API tokens in a single session, equating to 100 dollars per hour for a 100 dollar a month subscription—a massive subsidy. This shows why Anthropic would not want to subsidize programmatic usage, as it would massively cannibalize API revenue. Reports suggested that a 200 dollar subscription could allow for 2000 to 5000 dollars in compute. The general consensus has been that if you maxed out your Anthropic plan, they were effectively offering a 10X to 20X type of subsidy. They are not yet taking that subsidy away from their main accounts, but they are taking it away for usage that happens outside of their core ecosystem. This move is more about capacity constraints than developer relations.
The speaker dismisses the idea that Anthropic has unlimited compute after the SpaceX deal, stating that even hundreds of thousands of H100s and H200s are "a drop in the hat" given stratospherically growing demand, increasing inference costs, and the need to train next-generation competitive models. The speaker references the "semiconductor shortage until 2030," affecting memory, logic, ASML machines, TSMC fab capacity, and power infrastructure—all years-long bottlenecks. When supply is fixed but enterprise demand is exploding, consumers get rationed, and big companies are happy to pay for AI on a usage-based model.
The speaker agrees with the point that Open AI is also not going to offer such subsidies for long, and they will likely follow a similar model in the less than one-year range. We might need to prepare for a world where consumers rely more on open-source models running on their own hardware until that also gets supply constrained. Simply put, this situation was a complete inevitability. You cannot persist in a scenario of extremely limited compute and effectively unlimited and growing demand and expect tokens to stay subsidized, no matter how valuable the affinity of those who were once subsidized. Open AI will be forced to make a very similar decision before very long at all.
While Anthropic handled the communications poorly, alienating many, the real bummer is not just that certain services will cost more. It's that, in general, "the token maxing era is ending." We have had a very brief six-month golden window where coding models were good enough that we could create anything our little brains thought of without really having to worry about the costs. Now, because of the laws of physics and supply and demand, we are going to have to start to consider the cost of what we do. That's a bummer, but it is the reality.
The speaker advises that for now, if you're doing something that Anthropic doesn't particularly like or competes with their core services, run on over to CodeX and soak up as much subsidy as you can before they have to change. And for those using Claude even directly in the way that they want you to, do not assume that you're going to get a 10X subsidy forever either. It seems more likely than not that market forces will, over the next year, force even those subsidies to go away as well.
The times they are a-changing.

The Big Take This episode focuses on Generation Alpha, individuals born between 2010 and 2025, who are currently aged 1 to 16. It is the largest generation that has ever existed, making up about 25% of the population. Early concerns about this generation include their constant exposure to media, lack of a traditional "analog childhood," and potential impacts on development, with some educators reporting challenges in literacy and self-discipline. These worries are recognized as part of a recurring historical pattern where older generations scrutinize the youth. A defining characteristic of Generation Alpha is their advanced technological fluency. Komugiko 令和メガネ合戦: AI時代にキャリアをどう築くか？：Q&Aスペシャル in ゴールデンウィーク!! #コムギコ #78
本日、皆様にお届けするブリーフィングは、リスナーからの多岐にわたる質問と、AIがもたらす社会変革への深い洞察が凝縮された内容です。私たちは今、かつてない情報過多の時代に生きており、その中で自身のキャリアと生き方をどのように見定めるか、具体的な指針が求められています。
まず、さくさくさんの「言葉に表しにくい気持ち悪さ」という問いかけから、この時代が抱える構造的な課題が見えてきます。学生から見える社会の職業像は、テレビCMなどで認知度の高い消費財企業など、極めて限定的かつ偏った情報によって形成されているのが現状です。これは個人の問題ではなく、社会に情報が届く仕組みそのものに起因する構造的な不均衡であり、AI時代にはこの情報の非対称性がさらに加速していきます。
AIの進化は、私たちを取り巻く労働環境に劇的な変化をもたらしています。新卒の若手が行ってきた「下積み」の仕事、例えばコーディングの下準備やリサーチ、議事録作成といった定型業務は、AIが人間よりも圧倒的に早く低コストで代替し始めています。実際、大手テック企業や日本の大企業でも新卒採用の抑制や中途採用へのシフトが顕著です。特定のスキルが陳腐化するスピードは加速し、一つの専門スキルを何年もかけて磨き続ける従来のキャリアスタイルは、もはや「良いもの」では通用しなくなってきています。
このような変化の中で、私たちがどう生き、どう働くべきか。そこで提言されるのが、小麦さんの「自分が楽しいかどうか」を判断基準とする生き方です。これは単なる趣味嗜好ではなく、AI時代を生き抜くための戦略的な視点であると語られます。AIが効率や稼げる金額そのものを底上げし、誰もがそれなりの質の仕事をこなせるようになる未来において、差がつくのは「どれだけ長く、深く、その仕事を続けられるか」であり、それは最終的に「好きかどうか」に帰結するからです。
では、自分が本当に楽しいこと、没頭できることを見つけるにはどうすれば良いのでしょうか。 一つ目の鍵は「身体知」です。AIが統計的な「言語知」で世界を構成するのに対し、自分の足で動き、自分の目で見、自分の耳で聞いて初めて得られる「身体知」は、AIには決して再現できない、あなた独自の視点と洞察の源泉となります。学生のうちから、異なる業界や多様な人々と積極的に触れ合い、短期間のスポットワークなども活用して「食わず嫌い」をせずに多様な体験を積むことが推奨されます。
二つ目の鍵は「時間を忘れること」を観察することです。「何が好きか」という問いは意外と自分では答えにくいもの。それよりも、気がつくと2時間、3時間と没頭してしまっていること、あるいは特定の場所に行くと何だか楽しいと感じるような「無意識の反応」にこそ、あなたの深層的な興味が隠されています。日常の中で「この瞬間、時間を忘れているな」と感じる瞬間に意識を向けることで、AIには代えられない独自の価値創造へと繋がるヒントが見つかるでしょう。
AIは、私たちに心地よい答えを返す「思考ファンシー」という危険性も孕んでいます。AIが返す答えは、あくまで過去の膨大なデータから統計的に最もらしいとされる「言語知」の組み合わせであり、そこに「意志」「信念」「人格」はありません。AIの仕組みを知り、その限界を理解することで、私たちはAIが提供する「心地よいエコーチェンバー」にハックされることなく、自身の「思考の独立性」を保つことができるのです。
そして、リスナーの皆さんを「粉もの」と呼ぶ、という新たな試みが明かされました。これは、小麦という番組名にちなんだ、遊び心に満ちたリスナーとの繋がり方であり、番組がリスナーと共に「資本主義をハックする」というテーマを、互いに「練り上げ、発酵させていく」という意欲の表れでもあります。
AI時代は、私たち一人ひとりが自身の価値基準を深く問い直し、内発的な動機付けに基づいて行動することの重要性を浮き彫りにします。それは「AIに何ができるか」ではなく、「AIにできないことは何か」、そして「私は何に喜びを感じ、どう世界に関わるか」という、人間としての本質的な問いへと私たちを誘うものです。
以上で本日のブリーフィングを終了いたします。

The Economist The Intelligence: Fired alarm: AI hype versus labour-market history
Hello and welcome to The Intelligence. I am Host Name. Today on the show: the debate on AI's impact on the labor market, the scramble for Africa's critical minerals, and a profile of Japan's World Cup contenders.
First up, the future of work and artificial intelligence. Many workers and AI leaders express pessimism, predicting significant job displacement, with some polls suggesting one in five people fear losing their job to AI. However, experts argue that historical evidence, like the Industrial Revolution, shows new technologies rarely lead to widespread, immediate job loss as quickly as feared. The Industrial Revolution, though disruptive, saw real wages hold steady and the number of people in work nearly triple over a century. Even recent technological shifts in the mid-20th century, which caused high job disruption, are now seen as a "golden age" for workers.
Current data does not yet indicate an unprecedentedly disruptive shift due to AI. While graduate unemployment is up, this trend predates recent AI advancements. True, widespread disruption would involve extremely rapid productivity growth and broad job losses across all sectors, which are not presently observed. The doomsaying from AI leaders may stem from branding goals or a limited historical perspective rather than a clear view of future economic reality.
Next, we turn to the renewed global interest in Africa's critical minerals. In Western Tanzania, an untapped nickel deposit at the Kabanga mine has become a focus for Western nations seeking to reduce their reliance on China, which currently dominates the global nickel supply chain. The Tanzanian government also views this as a key economic project. The US is actively working to counter China's influence in Africa's mineral sector, using diplomatic pressure and conditional support to boost American firms' involvement.
China, previously the dominant player, is now adapting its strategy. Observing the renewed Western interest, Beijing is showing greater willingness to meet African governments' demands, particularly regarding in-country processing of raw materials. This addresses a long-standing African concern about merely exporting raw ore without adding value. While Africa has vast mineral wealth, realizing its full benefits requires robust infrastructure and policies that ensure extraction directly benefits African nations.
Finally, we head to Japan for a profile of their World Cup football team. Since 1998, Japan has consistently qualified for the World Cup, twice reaching the round of 16. Fans are optimistic, hoping for a top-eight finish. Under coach Hajime Moriyasu, Japan famously upset Germany and Spain in the last World Cup. However, the team faces challenges, with injuries to key players like captain Wataru Endo and star Kaoru Mitoma casting doubt on their participation. Japan will compete against Sweden, Tunisia, and the Netherlands in the group stage, aiming to win the championship. Football's popularity has surged in Japan since the J-League's inception in the 1990s, with passionate fans adopting vibrant traditions and even commissioning a J-Pop anthem for the team.
That's all for this episode of The Intelligence. We'll see you back here tomorrow.

New York Times The Daily: A New Leader — and a New Showdown — at the Fed
This episode of The Daily unpacks a dramatic chess match playing out at the highest levels of American economic policy, centered around the future of the Federal Reserve. For months, President Trump waged what was described as a long-simmering war against Fed Chair Jerome Powell, fueled by his demand for lower interest rates.
This pressure campaign wasn't subtle. At one point, a criminal investigation was launched into Powell, based on what were described as spurious renovation projects at the Fed's headquarters. Many saw this as politically motivated, an attempt to force Powell out. The pressure intensified to the point where a key Republican senator, Thom Tillis, indicated he wouldn't support Trump's nominee unless the investigation into Powell ceased. He wanted to avoid the perception of a fool at the Federal Reserve, especially during a time of high prices and economic uncertainty.
Ultimately, the investigation was dropped, and the path seemed clear for Trump to replace Powell with his chosen candidate, Kevin Warsh. But the drama didn't end there. As his term as chair concluded, Powell revealed his unexpected counter-move: he would remain a governor on the Fed's board. He saw this as his one tool of leverage, enabling him to block Trump from appointing another partisan ally to the seven-person board, thereby limiting Trump's overall influence over the institution. Powell stated he was literally staying because of the actions that had been taken, and that it was to protect the Fed from political attacks that were battering the institution.
This created a totally unusual scenario: both the old and new Fed chairs would be trying to coexist inside the central bank. The man Trump had lined up, Kevin Warsh, an avowed inflation hawk and a long-standing critic of the Fed's expansive balance sheet, now faced an immediate credibility test. Warsh had a history of pushing back on calls for interest rate cuts, always concerned about the risks of higher inflation. Yet, once he became Trump's nominee, his stance appeared to flip-flop, advocating for lower rates. This sudden shift raised uncomfortable questions about political motivation, suggesting he was adopting the president's policy lap dog role.
The overall narrative is one of a pivotal institution caught in a maelstrom of political pressure. The central question becomes whether the Fed can continue to make independent policy decisions, based purely on economic conditions, or if it will inevitably be politicized by intimidation and external pressure. Even Powell's principled decision to stay on, to protect the Fed's independence, ironically opens up criticism that he too has made a political decision, demonstrating just how deeply intertwined politics and central banking have become. The future holds an incredibly awkward environment within the central bank, with two powerful figures potentially at loggerheads, and the stakes for the economy couldn't be higher.

BBC World News Digest: 'It's an honour to be your friend' - Trump tells Xi
Welcome to the Global News Podcast from the BBC World Service.
Main stories in this edition:
US President Donald Trump held a high-stakes summit in Beijing with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The summit was dominated by issues of trade, Iran, Taiwan, and technology. An analyst noted that China knew how to make President Trump feel special and that Trump, in turn, offered glowing praise for President Xi. It was observed that Trump presented himself differently, seeking to be perceived as an equal rather than his usual bombastic self. On concrete outcomes, the summit was expected to yield symbolic gestures rather than massive trade deals. However, the optics were important for both governments, particularly regarding the future of the tariff war.
In the Middle East, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed to have made a secret trip to the United Arab Emirates during the Iran War to meet its president. His office stated the visit led to a historic breakthrough in relations. However, the Emirati state swiftly denied this happened, calling the claims baseless. An analyst suggested the statement from Netanyahu's office was about propaganda, while the UAE's denial stemmed from not wanting to provoke Iran, despite close business ties. Previous attempts by Netanyahu to visit the UAE had been cancelled due to local anger over events in Israel.
In Lebanon, the Health Ministry reported that 22 people, including eight children, were killed in Israeli airstrikes across the south of the country in the latest day of violence. Nearly three thousand people have been killed since the Iranian-backed armed group Hezbollah started firing at Israel in response to its war on Iran, with four hundred of those deaths occurring since the ceasefire came into effect less than a month ago. Israel has seized large swathes of South Lebanon and ordered residents to leave. A correspondent reported hearing continuous explosions and the buzz of an Israeli drone, noting that while the ceasefire was supposed to stop the war, it had not. Civilians were suffering, and many expressed support for Hezbollah, believing the group was defending their land.
Regarding the US-led peace plan for Gaza, the top diplomat overseeing it, Nikolai Mladenov, said he could see a role for Hamas as a political movement in the Palestinian territory, but only if it disarms. Mr. Mladenov clarified that a political party disavowing armed activity could compete in national elections, but armed factions or militias with their own military command and control systems could not exist alongside a transitional Palestinian Authority. Israel's government, however, stated that the terms of the peace deal banned Hamas from any role in governing Gaza. Hamas has so far refused to disarm. Mr. Mladenov stressed that both sides faced a choice: the peace plan or a permanent division of Gaza.
In the United States, the conviction of disgraced lawyer Alex Murdaugh for the murder of his wife and son was overturned by the State Supreme Court. The court ordered a new trial, citing that a local county clerk had unfairly biased the jury against him in the original trial. The trial had garnered intense interest, even inspiring a drama mini-series. The clerk in question also faced charges for publishing a tell-all book about the proceedings, which was later pulled due to plagiarism.
French President Emmanuel Macron's marriage has been the subject of intense interest. Last year, a video appeared to show his wife, Brigitte, slapping him. While they initially dismissed it as a joke, a French journalist has now claimed the reason was a jealous row over text messages exchanged between the President and an Iranian actress. The new book alleges that Macron sent messages, including one saying "I find you very pretty," and that Brigitte Macron was upset by what these messages suggested.
Finally, we look back at the life of Jason Collins, the NBA's first openly gay player, whose death at the age of 47 was announced on Tuesday. The NBA Commissioner stated that Collins' impact and influence extended far beyond basketball to make sports more inclusive. Collins first came out in 2013, writing an essay that famously began with the words "I am a 34-year-old NBA center, I am black, and I am gay." He later spoke about how his life had exponentially improved since coming out, and that he embraced the role of helping other athletes feel comfortable to step forward.
And that's all from us for now. Until next time, goodbye.

Good Morning from the Financial Times. Today is Thursday May 14th and this is your FT News Briefing.

Warsh, a former governor in the mid-2000s, is expected to be signed off by President Trump. He must sell over $130 million in assets before starting. J Powell could remain chair until then. Warsh takes the role as the American economy faces high inflation, with recent data showing sharp price rises.
The Bank of England is loosening its stance on crypto, preparing to water down planned restrictions on stablecoins. This follows criticism that the UK was too conservative. FT's Martin Arnold highlighted key revisions: softening individual and business holding limits, and potentially reducing a 40% asset deposit requirement at the central bank, which made the UK unattractive compared to the US. This pivot is driven by concern the UK might miss out on digital asset opportunities, as the US has "stolen a march" with its dollar-based stablecoin industry. Risks include potential outflow of deposits into stablecoins, weakening the banking system and credit flow. Also, over-investment in securities could increase volatility. Central bank deposits aim to provide security. Martin Arnold believes these changes will help attract digital investment. He notes UK banks' larger role in funding the economy (70-80% vs US's 30-40%) and a less liquid capital market compared to the US, necessitating caution.
The war in Iran is now impacting Germany's domestic politics. Support for the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has surged since it opposed the US-led conflict. The AfD, characterized as "really far-right" and historically campaigning on mass deportation, is now ahead of the ruling Christian Democrats. FT's Annelise Chasan explains the AfD, despite past MAGA alignment, is now distancing itself from Trump. The Iran war's economic impact, like rising fuel prices, is hurting Germans, a point the AfD quickly leveraged. In eastern Germany, where anti-American sentiment is deep-seated, the AfD's criticism of the US administration resonates. While Chancellor Merz also criticized the US conflict, only the AfD benefited. Merz faces criticism for the economy, with growth forecasts down to 0.5% due to the war. Despite being "taboo" and "extremist," the AfD could achieve an unprecedented breakthrough: winning a federal state (Saxony-Anhalt) in September, controlling its regional parliament, and having a prime minister sit on the Bundesrat. This would be a "big political earthquake."
Finally, growing expectations suggest Health Secretary Wes Streeting might challenge Keir Starmer's position as UK Prime Minister. Streeting, popular with gilt investors, is rumored to quit his current role and attempt to topple Starmer as early as today. Starmer has stated he won't back down.

Bloomberg The Big Take: The Russian Operation Using AI Fakes to Target Voters
Bloomberg Audio Studios presents The Big Take from Bloomberg News.
The podcast opens with a video of a man claiming Olena Zelenska, wife of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, purchased a Bugatti, welcoming her to the family. A 4.5 million euro receipt was shown. This caused scandal given Ukraine's war. However, investigative reporter Stephanie Baker found the video inconsistent and the invoice had misspellings. Bugatti confirmed the report was a fabrication, stating Zelenska was not a client. Despite Bugatti's denial, the false video spread widely, amplified by an influencer, contributing to other allegations of Zelenska's luxury spending.
This Bugatti video was part of a larger disinformation campaign. Stephanie Baker and Pre Benganini linked nearly 200 similar posts to Storm 1516, a Russian influence operation. Storm 1516 uses pro-Kremlin narratives, alleging corruption in Ukraine or among Western politicians. These unverified stories are presented as news reports or whistleblower accounts. Storm 1516 aims to sow doubt about figures like Zelenskyy and Western leaders, disrupting reality. The volume of this disinformation is increasing due to better AI and fewer online guardrails, doubling in the first quarter of this year.
Storm 1516 began in August 2023, after Elon Musk acquired X in October 2022 and dismantled content moderation. The operation first targeted Ukraine, aiming to hinder military aid. It then broadened to the US election, spreading fake stories about Kamala Harris, Tim Waltz, and illegal immigrant voting. After Trump's win, focus shifted to Europe, targeting leaders with corruption claims. None of these stories are true, including a ridiculous claim about President Macron building a bunker. Despite being fabricated, these narratives went viral.
Western officials believe Storm 1516 is backed by Russia's GRU military intelligence agency, specifically Unit 29155, responsible for sabotage and assassinations like Sergei Skripal's. The operation receives funding for servers and AI software. It's overseen by Putin's first deputy chief of presidential administration, Sergei Kiriyenko, who sets broad goals. Individual Russian operatives, including an ex-Florida cop, help execute it. Key to the operation are influencers who actively share Storm 1516 content.
Russia has a long history of disinformation. Now, it exploits AI and the lack of social media regulation. AI-doctored videos are increasingly sophisticated. X, once having good content moderation, now relies on community notes. However, less than 20% of Storm 1516's narratives were flagged. X did not comment. An X official mentioned 800 million accounts were removed in 2024, acknowledging a Russian campaign. While X removed about 20 identified Storm 1516 accounts, dozens of others spreading false material remain.
Storm 1516's goal is to promote a pro-Kremlin narrative: Ukraine and Europe are corrupt, support for Ukraine should end. They aim to undermine democracy in the US and Europe, seeing it as a threat to Putin. They act as "chaos agents" by encouraging questioning of established truths. This undermines politicians supporting Ukraine. While direct electoral impact is hard to prove, these narratives reinforce doubts about election fairness. They had success, like boosting anti-EU debates and the AFD's vote share in Germany. The Kremlin's spokesperson declined to comment.
The US has largely withdrawn from tech regulation and exposing nation-state disinformation, dismantling relevant agencies. In contrast, the EU fined X 120 million euros for misinformation, with an ongoing investigation, relying on the Digital Services Act. Stephanie Baker warns disinformation is a global problem, with a third of fabricated stories targeting elections. She expects aggressive targeting of future US midterms, concerned that without dedicated government agencies monitoring this, many will believe false narratives.

Today on the AI Daily Brief.

This early announcement signals a significant release, hinting at even more to come during the main IO event. This will roll out to the latest generation of Google and Samsung headsets over the summer, and will become available on smartwatches, glasses, and laptops later this year.
