BBC World News Digest: The Global Story: What Elon Musk did next
Welcome to this special audio briefing.
We begin with a look back at a cabinet meeting from February 2025 where then-President Trump asked Elon Musk to speak about his Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE. Trump praised Musk as a tremendously successful guy and tasked him with explaining how they were cutting federal spending.
Musk, not an official cabinet member but a special government employee, detailed ambitious plans to reduce the federal deficit by a trillion dollars, requiring daily savings of four billion dollars. He expressed confidence in achieving this. However, just months later, in May of last year, Musk left DOGE.
While he maintained a high public profile, he largely kept a low profile until recently, when a major lawsuit against OpenAI founder Sam Altman brought him back into the headlines. Our North America Technology Correspondent, Lily Jamali, has been covering this landmark trial in Oakland, California.
The lawsuit centers on the origins of OpenAI. Musk, Altman, and others co-founded OpenAI in 2015 as a non-profit organization dedicated to safely developing artificial intelligence for humanity's benefit. Musk himself donated around 38 million dollars to this venture. However, according to Musk's complaint, OpenAI later pivoted to a for-profit model, breaching its original mission and, in his view, allowing Altman and others to enrich themselves. This shift occurred around 2018, four years before OpenAI launched the massively successful ChatGPT.
Musk's end goals in the lawsuit are clear: he's seeking 150 billion dollars for OpenAI’s non-profit entity, the removal of Sam Altman as CEO, and the unwinding of OpenAI’s for-profit structure.
In court, the judge, Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, took a stern stance on social media. She explicitly told Musk to stop posting about the case on X, citing his disparaging remarks against Altman and other attempts to sway public opinion. She even extended the warning to Altman, who also agreed to cease his online commentary.
Musk's personal AI venture, XAI, and its controversial chatbot, Grok, have also been a focus. Grok has faced scrutiny for generating problematic content, including sexually explicit deepfakes. In court, Musk made the uncomfortable admission that he used OpenAI's models to train his own XAI products, leading critics to label this as hypocritical. Globally, XAI and Grok are under investigation by several dozen US state attorneys general and European authorities for their role in generating harmful content.
Beyond the courtroom drama, a more significant story is unfolding: Elon Musk's satellite internet company, Starlink. With around 10,000 satellites already in low Earth orbit, Starlink dominates the sector, serving over 10 million active users across 150 countries. It provides internet services to airlines, rural communities, and even disaster-stricken areas.
Crucially, Starlink has been deployed in war zones. During the Ukraine conflict, Musk controversially restricted Starlink's use, denying it to Ukrainian forces for an attack on Russian targets in Crimea, citing fears of nuclear escalation. Later, he also denied access to Russian forces. He has also made Starlink available in places like Venezuela and Iran, often following political maneuvers or internet blackouts.
Musk's ambitions for Starlink are vast. He recently sought permission to launch an additional one million satellites, envisioning them as space-based data centers powered by solar energy. This strategy aims to bypass Earth's power constraints for AI development. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, a competitor in the satellite internet space, has formally objected to Musk's plans.
In Washington, there's a growing realization that Musk's influence extends far beyond traditional politics. It's arguable that he holds more power than some heads of state. With no term limits and global reach, his ability to control internet access is a raw power that can be a matter of life or death, especially in conflict or disaster zones. Musk has been building this power infrastructure for years, and he will continue to shape global connectivity and technology long after current political leaders have left office.
Thank you for joining us. We'll talk to you again soon.

While President Trump sought to secure short-term trade wins to project strength domestically, President Xi was playing a longer game, subtly advancing China's vision for global dominance. The meeting underscored profound and unresolved geopolitical tensions, particularly in military, economic, and technological spheres, all complicated by President Trump's perceived weakened position due to the ongoing Iran conflict.
The 3 Key Insights
Our first key insight reveals President Trump's significantly weakened position and his focus on easily achievable outcomes. Unlike his triumphant visit in 2017, Trump arrived in Beijing under the cloud of an unresolved Iran conflict, which had defied his expectations of a swift resolution. Consequently, his primary objective was to secure immediate, tangible business deals – what are colloquially termed the "Three Bs": beef, beans, and Boeing. These are essentially routine American exports that China would purchase anyway, allowing Trump to declare easy "wins" back home without tackling more complex issues.
The second insight highlights the escalating and largely unaddressed fundamental divides between the two superpowers. Beyond the transactional trade discussions, the core issues of global leadership remain untouched. China is in the midst of a rapid expansion of its nuclear arsenal, aiming to achieve parity with the United States and Russia. Notably, Beijing steadfastly refuses any arms control negotiations until that goal is met. Concurrently, Taiwan's geopolitical status and the strength of the U.S. commitment to its defense stand as critical points of contention, with China subtly seeking diplomatic shifts that could undermine Taiwan's sovereignty.
Our third insight uncovers the urgent yet largely sidelined AI arms race. The burgeoning competition in artificial intelligence, exemplified by the development of potent cyberattack capabilities like 'Mythos,' represents an alarming new frontier of potential conflict. While both nations acknowledge the critical need for guardrails around AI, the Trump administration's initial "unfettered industry" approach, coupled with its distraction by unfolding events in the Middle East, meant it was largely ill-prepared for substantive engagement on AI regulation. This critical lack of engagement risks allowing a dangerous new threat to proliferate unchecked.
The 'So What?'
So, what does this all mean? This summit was less about resolving core bilateral issues and more about a strategic dance of geopolitical positioning amidst a landscape of increasing global instability. President Trump sought immediate, superficial "wins" to project an image of strength, particularly following the protracted Iran situation. In stark contrast, President Xi operated with a clear long-term vision. He aimed to demonstrate China as the stable, reliable global power of the future, quietly probing the depth of U.S. commitments to its allies and steadily preparing for a future where China is the undisputed global hegemon. The absence of substantive progress on critical issues such as nuclear arms control and AI governance leaves a perilous vacuum in global stability, intensifying an already tense rivalry.
The Golden Quote
To encapsulate the gravity of this situation, David Sanger provided a potent summary: "We all know there are much more fundamental divides between the two countries. Divides that go to the heart of the question of who will be the dominant economic power, the dominant military power, the dominant technological power for the next number of decades."

US inflation jumped to its highest level since two thousand twenty-three last month, primarily driven by soaring gas prices exacerbated by the war in Iran. This raises concerns about broader economic slowdown as consumer spending is impacted and the Federal Reserve's ability to cut interest rates is diminished, potentially leading to significant lost output.
Third, Blue Owl's Private Credit Challenges. The private credit market is showing signs of stress, exemplified by Blue Owl, where inflows into its largest fund have drastically declined. On May first, the fund reported only twenty-six million dollars in new investments, a ninety-five percent decrease from this time last year. This reflects broader investor concerns about advancements in artificial intelligence hitting software companies and the overall health of the private market, leading to partial redemption limits and liquidity pressures.
The 'So What?' The current economic environment presents a "perfect storm" of high inflation, rising borrowing costs, and potential economic slowdown. Governments and central banks face immense pressure to navigate these challenges without exacerbating market instability or undermining economic growth. For businesses, higher operational costs and reduced consumer demand pose significant threats, while political leaders will find that affordability issues deeply resonate with voters in upcoming elections. Wall Street Journal The Journal: The Vape Cloud Hanging Over the FDA
1. The Core Thesis
The abrupt resignation of FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary signals a significant political victory for the vaping industry and a dramatic shift in federal nicotine regulation. Driven by former President Trump's evolving stance on vaping to court young voters and the lobbying efforts of domestic vape companies, the FDA is now prioritizing market access over public health concerns, ushering in an era of less restrictive oversight for new nicotine products.
2. The 3 Key Insights
* Insight 1: Makary's Contrarian Stance. Dr. Marty Makary, a physician by training, consistently prioritized public health, particularly regarding the risks of flavored vaping products for young people. Despite pressure from the White House and industry, he stalled applications for fruit-flavored vapes, viewing them as a "huge public health risk" and not wanting to be "the doctor who allowed those" onto the market. This principled stand, however, put him directly at odds with the incoming political agenda.
* Insight 2: Trump's Strategic Pivot on Vaping. Donald Trump's position on vaping underwent a significant transformation. Initially a critic who signed legislation to raise the tobacco purchasing age, his 2024 presidential campaign saw a strategic pivot. Advised that "saving vaping" could appeal to young MAGA voters, he publicly embraced the vaping industry, framing it as a fight against "big government" overreach and a means to help people quit smoking. This political alignment directly fueled the pressure on the FDA.
* Insight 3: The "Glass" Test Case and Regulatory Capitulation. The vaping company Glass became a pivotal test case. Despite developing an age-gated vape, their application for fruit flavors was stalled by Makary. However, following Trump's direct intervention and expressed frustration over the FDA's slow pace, Makary was out, and Glass's fruit-flavored products were swiftly approved. This shift culminated in a new FDA policy allowing all nicotine products with pending applications to be marketed immediately, effectively bypassing the traditional scientific review process and clearing the path for a "flood of new products."
3. The 'So What?'
This leadership change and policy shift at the FDA will have profound implications for both public health and the nicotine industry. For consumers, particularly young people, it means a vastly expanded market of new, potentially unvetted vaping products, many in appealing flavors. Public health advocates fear a new wave of nicotine addiction. For the vaping industry, it represents an unprecedented opening to rapidly introduce products to market without prior rigorous scientific approval, reshaping the competitive landscape and challenging the FDA's historical role as a gatekeeper of public safety. This moves the US further away from robust, science-led regulation in this sector.
4. The Golden Quote
Our reporter, Liz Essley White, on the future of FDA regulation: "This promise that the Trump White House has made to the vaping industry of saving vaping is not something that is going to be negotiable for the next Commissioner."

Harvard Business Review Cold Call: Microsoft’s Path to Adopting and Scaling AI Across its Sales Organization
Welcome to this Cold Call audio briefing.
This episode delves into the real-world challenges of deploying artificial intelligence, using Microsoft's rollout of CoPilot to its global salesforce as a prime example. The core thesis isn't about whether AI technology works – it does, and Microsoft built it. Instead, the central challenge revolves around the human, organizational, and behavioral layers essential for successful AI adoption and transformation. It highlights that integrating powerful, general-purpose AI into everyday work is far more complex than a simple technological deployment.
We extracted three key insights from this fascinating discussion.
1. The 'General-Purpose Paradox': Unlike previous targeted technologies, AI like CoPilot is general-purpose, meaning users aren't explicitly told how to use it. This demands a shift towards experimentation and discovery to find high-value use cases. However, traditional sales roles, driven by quotas, often leave little room for unstructured play and exploration, leading to a significant drop in initial adoption.
2. The 'Productivity J-Curve' and 'Competency Trap': New technology adoption often causes an initial dip in productivity, known as the J-curve, before benefits are realized. Many users abandon the tool during this dip. Additionally, highly skilled, experienced employees who are already efficient with existing systems may find their established workflows disrupted by new AI, making them initially less productive – a phenomenon termed the competency trap.
3. The Power of Social and Management Levers: Successful adoption requires more than just product and process. Microsoft learned that management support, which means not penalizing employees for initial productivity drops during the learning phase, is crucial. Even more powerful is leveraging social influence through 'adoption champions' – respected, often senior, but initially skeptical individuals who, when convinced, carry immense credibility and encourage broader peer adoption. Creating safe, off-task spaces for experimentation also proved vital.
The implications are profound for any organization considering large-scale AI deployment. First, understand that general-purpose AI demands a culture of experimentation and exploration, not just prescriptive training. Second, anticipate and proactively manage the inevitable initial dip in productivity and the potential resistance from highly competent employees. Leadership must support the learning curve and provide safe environments for discovery. Finally, harness the power of social networks and internal champions, especially those who can bridge the gap between tech enthusiasm and established work practices, to build trust and drive organic adoption. This comprehensive approach enables AI to elevate roles from transactional to more consultative, fostering innovation and higher-value work within the organization.
As Professor Xunyun Zhang succinctly puts it, "The gap is really between a great demo and a real workday."
Thank you for tuning into this audio briefing.

Our guests highlighted how AI acts as an "infinitely patient tutor," capable of guiding individuals through intricate scientific experiments—like assembling viruses—even if they've never held a pipette. This capability effectively overcomes the traditional bottleneck of human expertise, empowering even "novices" to achieve capabilities once reserved for a select few. Assets historically sought during times of crisis—such as gold, the US dollar, and government bonds—are proving to be less reliable than expected. Gold, for instance, had already rocketed in value before the current conflicts, causing it to fall alongside stocks when the latest tensions arose, behaving more like a speculative asset. The dollar, too, has shown vulnerability, and even government bonds, usually a refuge, are impacted by soaring inflation and governments' own heavy borrowing. These shifts challenge the fundamental role these assets play in investor portfolios.
Thirdly, despite these profound threats and economic uncertainties, stock markets continue to display an almost unwarranted optimism. Faced with significant global upheavals, including recent oil shocks from the Iran war, equity markets remain robust, often at all-time highs. This seems driven by a "muscle memory" developed from previous crises, where share prices, after initial plunges, recovered with remarkable speed. Investors who previously sold out when times seemed dire often missed significant rebounds. However, our analysis suggests that current disruptions might be more structural and permanent, making this prevailing bullish sentiment a potential precursor to a market bubble.
So what does this mean for us? We are at a critical juncture where the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence demands proactive, intelligent regulation to mitigate biological risks that could otherwise be democratized to devastating effect. Simultaneously, the unpredictable performance of traditional safe havens forces a fundamental re-evaluation of financial security. This new reality requires both policymakers and individual investors to discard outdated assumptions and embrace a more agile, forward-looking approach to navigating an increasingly complex and interconnected world.

The Journal: An AI Reality Check Date: Monday, May 11
Welcome to The Journal. Today, we delve into the pervasive influence of Artificial Intelligence, moving beyond the hype to understand its real-world impact. Our guide is Joanna Stern, an Emmy-award-winning tech journalist who undertook a year-long experiment, allowing AI and robots to govern nearly every aspect of her life for her upcoming book, "I Am Not a Robot."
1. The Core Thesis: Stern's compelling journey reveals a transformative era where AI is redefining our daily existence, from personal productivity to healthcare. Her core thesis underscores that while AI promises unparalleled advancements, it simultaneously introduces profound challenges concerning human cognition, critical discernment, and the very nature of our relationships. We are at a pivotal technological shift, akin to the dawn of the internet or the smartphone, demanding a clear-eyed assessment of AI's true capabilities and limitations.
2. The 3 Key Insights:
First, AI's immediate and most practical application lies in its capacity as a professional assistant. Stern found that AI-powered tools significantly enhanced her work performance and efficiency, proving to be an invaluable aid for managing tasks and reminders. This domain, encompassing everything from basic organizational tasks to complex data synthesis, highlights AI's current strength in augmenting human productivity, not merely replacing it. However, the line between assistance and over-reliance necessitates careful navigation.
Second, AI demonstrates remarkable potential in critical decision-making fields, particularly in healthcare. In radiology, for instance, AI can analyze complex medical images at a pixel level, detecting anomalies that human eyes might miss. Stern's personal experience with AI reviewing her mammogram showed it could flag potential concerns, prompting doctors to re-examine and ultimately leading to more thorough care. This underscores AI's role not as a substitute for human expertise, but as a powerful diagnostic co-pilot, enhancing accuracy and potentially saving lives by working in tandem with medical professionals.
Finally, the pervasive integration of AI raises significant concerns about the "atrophy of cognition" and the erosion of critical thinking, especially for younger generations. Stern's experiment revealed that relying on AI for tasks like college homework could bypass the fundamental learning process that develops analytical skills. Moreover, AI's tendency to "hallucinate" – presenting confident but false information – necessitates a heightened sense of digital literacy. As evidenced by her son's interaction with a chatbot diagnosing his praying mantis as pregnant (when it was simply dying), teaching children to question and verify AI-generated content is paramount to prevent them from accepting digital untruths as reality.
3. The 'So What?': The profound implications of AI's rise demand proactive engagement. As this technology becomes increasingly sophisticated and seamlessly integrated into our lives, we must cultivate a discerning relationship with it. This involves understanding AI's practical benefits, leveraging its power to enhance human capabilities in fields like medicine, and critically, safeguarding our intellectual independence and human connections. Establishing clear boundaries for AI's role in education and personal development is essential to ensure that we remain the architects of our future, not passive recipients of an AI-driven one.
4. The Golden Quote: To encapsulate this profound shift, Joanna Stern offers a stark warning about the future of human connection: "Human relationships have to have friction. They just naturally do, right? Humans are complicated. AI will tell us everything we want to hear, it is a mirror of ourselves in some ways. And if we raise kids that think that all interaction is just going to be easy and these things should pander to us, then that's not life, that's not a human experience."

Bloomberg The Big Take: Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell’s Legacy
## The Big Take: Jerome Powell's Tenure at the Fed (Briefing Script)
[SECTION] 1. The Core Thesis
Today's episode of "The Big Take" from Bloomberg News delves into the complex and often contentious tenure of Jerome Powell as Chair of the Federal Reserve. We explore how Powell, initially seen as a non-traditional pick, navigated unprecedented challenges, from the global financial crisis aftermath to the COVID-19 pandemic and surging inflation, all while facing persistent political pressure from the Trump administration. The core thesis is that Powell's legacy will ultimately be defined by his forceful defense of the Fed's independence and his eventual, albeit delayed, shift in monetary policy to combat inflation, despite the criticisms and challenges he encountered.
[SECTION] 2. The 3 Key Insights
[HEADING] Key Insight 1: A Non-Traditional Fed Chair Facing Unprecedented Political Pressure
Powell's journey to the Fed Chair was unusual. Unlike many of his predecessors, he was not a PhD economist, coming instead from law and private equity. This background initially drew attention but became less remarkable when looking further back in history. He was appointed as a Fed Governor by President Obama in 2012, then nominated as Chair by President Trump in 2017. However, Trump's initial support quickly soured, leading to an unprecedented campaign of public criticism and pressure on Powell and the Fed. Trump repeatedly called Powell "too late," "slow," and even explored firing him. This constant political interference created a unique challenge for Powell, forcing him to vigorously defend the Fed's institutional independence in a way no previous Chair had.
[HEADING] Key Insight 2: Navigating Crises: From Stagnation to Inflation
Powell's tenure spanned two major economic crises. During his early years as a governor under Obama, the US economy was still recovering from the 2008 financial crisis, marked by sluggish growth and stubbornly low inflation. The Fed's primary concern was boosting employment and preventing deflation, maintaining near-zero interest rates for an extended period. This experience deeply influenced Powell, leading him to advocate for a "big and aggressive fiscal response" when the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020. The Fed moved swiftly, lowering interest rates to zero and unleashing a host of special lending facilities. However, as the economy emerged from the pandemic, inflation surged. Initially, the Fed, influenced by traditional economic theory and the 2008 experience, categorized this inflation as "transitory," primarily due to supply shocks that were expected to naturally abate. This proved to be a critical misstep, leading to accusations of being "late to raise interest rates" and a subsequent loss of credibility.
[HEADING] Key Insight 3: The Imperative of Independence and a Policy Pivot
The sustained political attacks from Trump and the later misjudgment on inflation's transience presented a dual challenge to Powell's leadership and the Fed's credibility. The episode highlights how Powell, despite his non-economist background, worked tirelessly to understand economic theory and develop a consensus-building approach within the Fed. His response to Trump's attempts to politicize monetary policy, even when facing a potential criminal investigation by the DOJ over a headquarters renovation, was a defiant stand for the institution's independence. This culminated in him publicly stating he would not be bullied. Moreover, the Fed eventually pivoted on its "transitory" stance, acknowledging the persistence of inflation and beginning aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022. This shift, though late, reflected a recognition of the need to address the real economic impact on Americans, who were deeply concerned about affordability and rising prices, a factor that even influenced political outcomes like the 2024 (simulated) election.
[SECTION] 3. The 'So What?'
So what does this mean for the future of central banking and the US economy? Powell's legacy, while marked by the inflation miss, will likely be dominated by his firm resolve in defending the Fed's independence against unprecedented political interference. This sets a critical precedent, signaling to future presidents and global central banks alike that political pressure should not dictate monetary policy. The delayed response to inflation, however, serves as a stark reminder of the challenges in real-time economic forecasting and the potential costs of misjudgment, particularly for the most vulnerable. It also highlights the growing importance of fiscal policy in conjunction with monetary policy during crises. Going forward, the Fed will face immense pressure to restore its anti-inflation credibility, and any future challenges to its independence will be viewed through the lens of Powell's battle with Trump. The world is watching closely, understanding that the independence of the world's most powerful central bank has global repercussions, influencing everything from international financial stability to democratic governance models.
[SECTION] 4. The Golden Quote
"Fed chairs are usually judged in history by their performance on inflation. And if you judge Chair Powell on inflation, you could argue that he hasn't done the best. But I think that because he is now viewed as this person who has stood up to President Trump and taken extraordinary steps to defend Fed independence and to make it clear to the American people how important Fed independence is, I think that is arguably going to be how he is most remembered."
